notes.text: In the cloudy and dark day — In the time of general distress.
The fat — The powerful and rich. I will feed - I will judge and punish them.
I will judge — I will vindicate the poor. The fat cattle - The rich. The lean - The poor.

One shepherd — Christ, the great good, chief, only shepherd, that laid down his life for his sheep. My servant David - The seed of David, the beloved one, who was typified by David, and is in other places called by his name, as Jer. xxx, 9 chap. xxxvii, 24 Isaiah xxxvii, 35 Hosea iii, 5. He shall feed - Do all the office of a good and faithful shepherd, and that forever.
My servant — Christ was in this great work his fathers servant, Isaiah xlii, 1.

glossa.text:
*A psalm in confession.* Confession is twofold; one is of praise, the other of sins. The confession of praise befits the perfect, the confession of sins those who are beginning *inicipientibus*; whence in this psalm the prophet admonishes to confession. ((CASS.)) This psalm teaches both to praise God unceasingly, and unceasingly to bewail our sins: because neither in evils is one to despair, nor in good things ought the mind to be lifted up. First he enjoins upon the perfect the chief kind of confession, that is, praise.

*Rejoice ye.* ((AUG.)) If the voice rejoices outwardly, etc., *as far as* and in what order and how wonderfully he made it. *All the earth.* Admonishing to praise. Not one corner of the earth does he exhort: but as he knows the blessing to have been sown everywhere, so from everywhere he requires jubilation. *Serve ye in gladness.* ((AUG.)) This servitude is not of bitterness, nor of indignation, but of happiness and of liberty. Let charity therefore make thee a servant, because truth has made thee free. Whence the Lord: *If you shall abide in my word, you shall be my disciples indeed: and you shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free ((Joan. VIII))*. 

*In gladness.* Because they are set free; not murmuring, as in the desert: whence he subjoins the reward.

*Enter ye into his sight.* It is a great thing to rejoice in the sight of so great a one. *Enter ye in.* ((CASS.)) Secondly, to those about to enter, the second kind of confession; nor let it be doubted, because mercy is with him.

notes.text: Since I heard of your faith and love — That is, of their perseverance and increase therein.
I cease not — In all my solemn addresses to God. To give thanks for you, making mention of you in my prayers - So he did of all the churches, Col. i, 9.

That the Father of that infinite glory which shines in the face of Christ, from whom also we receive the glorious inheritance, ver. 18, may give you the Spirit of wisdom and Revelation — The same who is the Spirit of promise is also, in the progress of the faithful, the Spirit of wisdom and Revelation; making them wise unto salvation, and revealing to them the deep things of God. He is here speaking of that wisdom and Revelation which are common to all real Christians.

The eyes of your understanding — It is with these alone that we discern the things of God. Being first opened, and then enlightened - By his Spirit. That ye may know what is the hope of his calling - That ye may experimentally and delightfully know what are the blessings which God has called you to hope for by his word and his Spirit. And what is the riches of the glory of his inheritance in the saints - What an immense treasure of blessedness he hath provided as an inheritance for holy souls.

And what the exceeding greatness of his power toward us who believe — Both in quickening our dead souls, and preserving them in spiritual life. According to the power which he exerted in Christ, raising him from the dead - By the very same almighty power whereby he raised Christ; for no less would suffice.

And he hath seated him at his own right hand — That is, he hath exalted him in his human nature, as a recompence for his sufferings, to a quiet, everlasting possession of all possible blessedness, majesty, and glory.

Far above all principality, and power, and might, and dominion — That is, God hath invested him with uncontrollable authority over all demons in hell, all angels in heaven, and all the princes and potentates on earth. And every name that is named - We know the king is above all, though we cannot name all the officers of his court. So we know that Christ is above all, though we are not able to name all his subjects. Not only in this world, but also in that which is to come - The world to come is so styled, not because it does not yet exist, but because it is not yet visible. Principalities and powers are named now; but those also who are not even named in this world, but shall be revealed in the world to come, are all subject to Christ.

And he hath given him to be head over all things to the church — An head both of guidance and government, and likewise of life and influence, to the whole and every member of it. All these stand in the nearest union with him, and have as continual and effectual a communication of activity, growth, and strength from him, as the natural body from its head.

The fulness of him that filleth all in all — It is hard to say in what sense this can be spoken of the church; but the sense is easy and natural, if we refer it to Christ, who is the fulness of the Father.

glossa.text: *Therefore.* The benefits conferred upon the human race, or upon the apostles, or upon the Ephesians having been enumerated, the Apostle subjoins what he thinks concerning their benefits, namely that he gives thanks, and asks that more be added, lest they be proud, but stretch beyond.
*That God,* etc. As if he should say: to obtain it I put forward not merits, but that he is God and the Father of Christ, etc.

*The eyes of the heart.* In his own image, therefore, know thou its author, who is not attained by bodily sense. Do not, therefore, think that God is attained by bodily sense, but with the eyes of the mind hear him. In the body, where the members are diverse, thou hearest in one place, thou seest in another. But in thy heart, where diverse members are not found, there thou hearest where thou seest. And to this end may he enlighten the eyes. *That you may know,* etc. This he says that they may be the more inclined: because when they shall fully know what the fruit of believers is, they will become the more inclined toward the cultivating of religion. Or thus: that hope be taken properly. And the sense is: That you may know what it is, namely his will *voluntas*; read *vocatio*, "calling", that is, how much the hope of eternal life avails, unto which he calls. And that you may know what the fulfilment of that hope is. Which he thus says: *And what are the riches.* Here he discloses what he understood by the name of hope: for he takes hope as the thing hoped for.

*What is the exceeding greatness.* The highest doctors shall have a certain increase of glory, beyond that which all shall have in common. For all shall have the same penny. *But star differeth from star in brightness ((I Cor. XV))*. *And there shall be diverse mansions in the house of the Father ((Joan. XIV))*.

*Raising him up,* etc. Now the example of the glory of the saints consists in the resurrection of the Saviour, that in it the faithful may know what has been promised to them. *At his right hand.* The right hand is the eternal beatitude which is given to the saints: the left is the misery which is given to the wicked. For by no form of body is God bounded and enclosed.

*Above every,* etc. This he says on account of the incarnation of the Son of God, that even having been made man he may be said to be above all the heavens, and above every creature, having his name by nature, not by adoption.

*Under his feet,* etc. By the feet full subjection is noted, and all things are deservedly subject to him, because they were made through him; or, the feet signify the humanity, because as the foot is the lower part of the body, so in Christ the lower nature is the humanity, which even the angels adore. *And him,* etc. After he has commemorated the dignity of Christ, he returns to us, showing that his dignity pertains to us; as if he should say: God so exalted Christ that this his exaltation pertains to us: because he himself is the head, and we the body, that we may partake of him. *The head.* According to the deity: because all were made by him, and also according to the humanity, by which the Church is joined to him, by nature and by grace. *For of his fullness we have all received ((Joan. X))*.

*His fullness.* Because he is filled up through them, yet being all things in all, here and in the time to come. Likewise. When those who have entered unto confession bend the knee to Christ, he is filled up, because those who withdraw seem to empty him. *All things in all.* Because the members confer nothing upon him, but he himself all things upon the members: because by his power they are what they are.

notes.text: Inherit the kingdom — Purchased by my blood, for all who have believed in me with the faith which wrought by love. Prepared for you - On purpose for you. May it not be probably inferred from hence, that man was not created merely to fill up the places of the fallen angels?

I was hungry, and ye gave me meat; I was thirsty, and ye gave me drink — All these works of outward mercy suppose faith and love, and must needs he accompanied with works of spiritual mercy. But works of this kind the Judge could not mention in the same manner. He could not say, I was in error, and ye recalled me to the truth; I was in sin, and ye brought me to repentance. In prison - Prisoners need to be visited above all others, as they are commonly solitary and forsaken by the rest of the world.

Then shall the righteous answer — It cannot be, that either the righteous or the wicked should answer in these very words. What we learn herefrom is, that neither of them have the same estimation of their own works as the Judge hath.
Inasmuch as ye did it to one of the least of these my brethren, ye did it to me — What encouragement is here to assist the household of faith? But let us likewise remember to do good to all men.
Depart into the everlasting fire, which was prepared for the devil and his angels — Not originally for you: you are intruders into everlasting fire.
Then will they answer — So the endeavour to justify themselves, will remain with the wicked even to that day!

And these shall go away into everlasting punishment, but the righteous into life everlasting — Either therefore the punishment is strictly eternal, or the reward is not: the very same expression being applied to the former as to the latter. The Judge will speak first to the righteous, in the audience of the wicked. The wicked shall then go away into everlasting fire, in the view of the righteous. Thus the damned shall see nothing of the everlasting life; but the just will see the punishment of the ungodly. It is not only particularly observable here

1. That the punishment lasts as long as the reward; but,

2. That this punishment is so far from ceasing at the end of the world, that it does not begin till then.

glossa.text: *And when.* Being about to be delivered to the cross very soon, he set before them the glory of him who triumphs, that he might make up by this promise for the scandals that were to follow. After the parables about the end of the world, the Lord now sets forth the manner of the judgment to come.

*The sheep from,* etc. There shall be two orders in the judgment, namely of the elect and of the reprobate: but of the elect some shall judge, to whom it is said: *You also shall sit upon twelve seats, judging the tribes of Israel.* Others shall be judged, to whom it is said: *I was hungry and you gave me to eat.* Likewise of the reprobate, some who are outside the Church shall not be judged: others who shall be judged, to whom it is said: *I was hungry, and you gave me not to eat,* etc.
*The goats.* The he-goat is a butting and rank-smelling animal, which was offered for sins in the law, and it signifies sinners: nor does he say she-goats, which can have young.

*Blessed of the Father.* Advanced by the benefit of my Father to the obtaining of glory, in which you may reign without corruption, to which you have been predestined from the foundation of the world.

*Then shall they answer.* Not distrusting the words of the Lord, but either amazed at the greatness of the king's majesty; or because every good thing that they did seems little to them, whence it is said: *The sufferings of this time are not worthy to be compared with the glory to come ((Rom. VIII))*, etc.
*Of these brethren.* My brethren and my mother are they who do the will of my Father.
*You gave me not,* etc. What does he deserve who has seized what belongs to another, if he is eternally damned who has not given anything of his own?

*Lord, when,* etc. They busy themselves to excuse themselves, as though they who were deceiving men could deceive God. But they have no excuse who would not be converted from evils and do alms; whence he adds: *As long as you did it not to one,* etc.

*Into everlasting punishment.* In vain therefore does Origen promise deliverance after many years to evil men and to the demons themselves. *Into everlasting punishment. ((AUG.))* In which matter Origen was assuredly the more merciful, who believed that the devil himself too and his angels, after punishments heavier according to their deserts and of longer duration, were to be rescued out of those torments and joined to the holy angels. But the Church has not undeservedly condemned him, both for this and for sundry other things, and chiefly for the blessednesses and miseries alternating without ceasing, and for the endless goings and returnings from those to these at fixed intervals of ages.

hymns.title: Lift up your heads, ye mighty gates
Who is the King of glory
The Lord reigns, the Lord reigns
Filled with excitement, all the happy throng (Mantos y palmas esparciendo)
Hail to the Lord's Anointed, great David's greater Son

praise.title: O Praise Him (All This for a King)

Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: The Spirit of Yahweh will rest on him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and of the fear of Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'A spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him' draws on the Messianic 'Spirit of the LORD... the spirit of wisdom and understanding... the spirit of knowledge.' Volume is strong (spirit + wisdom + knowledge in sequence); thematic coherence (the endowing Spirit granting wisdom and knowledge of God) and the passage's Messianic availability make this a high-confidence allusion.

echoes.text: He changes the times and the seasons; he removes kings, and sets up kings; he gives wisdom to the wise, and knowledge to those who have understanding; he reveals the deep and secret things; he knows what is in the darkness, and the light dwells with him.
echoes.note: 'A spirit of wisdom and revelation' coheres with Daniel's God who 'gives wisdom to the wise... reveals deep and hidden things.' Recurrence of the Danielic wisdom/revelation pairing (cf. 1:9 mystery) supports a medium echo; the volume is moderate alongside the dominant Isaiah 11 source.

echoes.text: For this cause I prayed, and understanding was given me: I called upon God, and there came to me a spirit of wisdom.
echoes.note: 'I prayed, and understanding was given me; I called, and the spirit of wisdom came to me' (deuterocanonical) closely parallels praying for 'a spirit of wisdom' to know God. Thematic coherence is strong and the Wisdom tradition was available in Greek-speaking Judaism; medium because it is a parallel within a shared milieu rather than a citation.

echoes.text: You shall speak to all who are wise-hearted, whom I have filled with the spirit of wisdom, that they make Aaron’s garments to sanctify him, that he may minister to me in the priest’s office.
echoes.note: God filling artisans with a 'spirit of wisdom' to equip them is one OT background for Spirit-given wisdom granted to God's people. Availability is real but thematic coherence with revelatory knowledge of God is weaker than Isaiah 11; marked low and contested.

echoes.text: He filled them with the knowledge of wisdom, And showed them good and evil. He set his eye upon their hearts, To show them the majesty of his works.
echoes.note: Sirach's depiction of God enlightening humans with knowledge and 'setting his eye on their hearts' resonates faintly with 'the eyes of your hearts enlightened.' Availability within the wisdom corpus is genuine; volume and verbal overlap are low, so the echo is contested.

echoes.text: Yahweh’s precepts are right, rejoicing the heart. Yahweh’s commandment is pure, enlightening the eyes.
echoes.note: 'The commandment of the LORD is pure, enlightening the eyes' offers an OT idiom of divine illumination behind 'the eyes of your hearts enlightened.' Thematic coherence (God enlightening the perceiving faculty) is plausible; volume is faint, so low and contested.

echoes.text: Yahweh says to my Lord, “Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool for your feet.”
echoes.note: 'Made him to sit at his right hand in the heavenly places, far above all rule and authority' reproduces 'Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies your footstool.' Volume is very high (the most-cited OT verse in the NT); recurrence and thematic coherence (enthroned exaltation over all powers) make this a near-quotation undergirding the entire exaltation statement.

echoes.text: You make him ruler over the works of your hands. You have put all things under his feet:
echoes.note: 'He put all things in subjection under his feet' is a verbatim citation of 'you have put all things under his feet.' Volume is maximal (direct verbal match); recurrence (1 Cor 15:27; Heb 2:8) and thematic coherence (the dominion granted to the exalted man over creation) make this an explicit quotation.

echoes.text: Yahweh says to my Lord, “Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool for your feet.”
echoes.note: 'He put all things in subjection under his feet' also fulfills Psalm 110:1's 'until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet,' which Ephesians conflates with Psalm 8:6. The footstool/subjection imagery shows the two enthronement psalms read together; volume and thematic coherence (subjugation of enemies under the exalted Lord) are high.

echoes.text: so that the priests could not stand to minister by reason of the cloud; for Yahweh’s glory filled Yahweh’s house.
echoes.note: 'The fullness of him who fills all in all' evokes the glory of the LORD filling the temple so that 'the priests could not stand to minister.' Thematic coherence (divine presence filling God's house, now the church as body/temple) is strong; medium because the link is conceptual and joins other temple-glory texts.

echoes.text: Can any hide himself in secret places so that I shall not see him? says Yahweh. Don’t I fill heaven and earth? says Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'Do I not fill heaven and earth? says the LORD' supplies the divine self-description behind 'him who fills all in all.' Thematic coherence with God's omnipresent fullness is strong; the volume is moderate (a shared plerosis motif), so medium confidence.

echoes.text: In the year that king Uzziah died, I saw the Lord sitting on a throne, high and lifted up; and his train filled the temple. Above him stood the seraphim. Each one had six wings. With two he covered his face. With two he covered his feet. With two he flew. One called to another, and said, “Holy, holy, holy, is Yahweh of Armies! The whole earth is full of his glory!”
echoes.note: 'The whole earth is full of his glory,' with the temple filled by the LORD's train, reinforces the fullness/glory imagery of 1:23. Availability and thematic coherence (glory filling the sanctuary) support a faint echo; volume is low alongside 1 Kings 8 and Jeremiah 23, so contested.

echoes.text: Yahweh, our Lord, how majestic is your name in all the earth, who has set your glory above the heavens!
echoes.note: 'Head over all things' resonates with Psalm 8's exaltation of God's name 'above the heavens' and the dominion theme framing the quoted v.6. Thematic coherence (universal supremacy) is plausible; the volume is low and the link secondary to 8:6, so contested.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.
echoes.note: The Son of Man coming in glory and seated on his throne, before whom all nations/peoples are gathered to serve him, is the direct backbone of v.31-32. Daniel's 'one like a son of man' receives dominion, glory, and kingdom over all peoples, nations, and languages; Matthew transposes this enthronement into the scene of universal judgment.

echoes.text: As for you, O my flock, thus says the Lord Yahweh: Behold, I judge between sheep and sheep, the rams and the male goats.
echoes.note: 'I judge between sheep and sheep, between rams and goats' is the explicit verbal and conceptual source for 'he will separate them... as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats' (v.32-33). The shepherd-judge distinguishing the flock animals is unmistakable.

echoes.text: Therefore thus says the Lord Yahweh to them: Behold, I, even I, will judge between the fat sheep and the lean sheep. Because you thrust with side and with shoulder, and push all the diseased with your horns, until you have scattered them abroad; therefore will I save my flock, and they shall no more be a prey; and I will judge between sheep and sheep.
echoes.note: The LORD 'will judge between the fat sheep and the lean sheep,' saving the weak from those who shove with side and shoulder. This grounds the criterion of judgment on treatment of the vulnerable and the shepherd-king's vindication of the mistreated, mirrored in care for the hungry, naked, sick, and imprisoned.

echoes.text: I will set up one shepherd over them, and he shall feed them, even my servant David; he shall feed them, and he shall be their shepherd. I, Yahweh, will be their God, and my servant David prince among them; I, Yahweh, have spoken it.
echoes.note: The promise of one shepherd, 'my servant David,' set over the flock as prince, is typologically fulfilled in the Son of Man / King who shepherds and judges the nations. The Davidic shepherd-king of Ezekiel 34 is the figure Matthew casts Jesus as embodying.

echoes.text: Isn’t it to distribute your bread to the hungry, and that you bring the poor who are cast out to your house? When you see the naked, that you cover him; and that you not hide yourself from your own flesh?
echoes.note: The acts of true fasting/righteousness — 'share your bread with the hungry, bring the homeless poor into your house, when you see the naked, cover him' — closely match the King's catalog of hungry/stranger/naked in v.35-36. Isaiah 58 is the strongest verbal parallel for the works that mark the righteous.

echoes.text: I will gather all nations, and will bring them down into the valley of Jehoshaphat; and I will execute judgment on them there for my people, and for my heritage, Israel, whom they have scattered among the nations. They have divided my land,
echoes.note: 'I will gather all the nations... and I will enter into judgment with them there' supplies the assize of the nations gathered before the throne (v.32), where they are judged on how they treated God's people.

echoes.text: “Let the nations arouse themselves, and come up to the valley of Jehoshaphat; for there will I sit to judge all the surrounding nations.
echoes.note: 'Let the nations be roused and come up to the valley of Jehoshaphat, for there I will sit to judge all the surrounding nations.' The enthroned divine Judge seated to judge the assembled nations directly parallels the Son of Man sitting on the throne of his glory to judge all the nations.

echoes.text: You shall flee by the valley of my mountains; for the valley of the mountains shall reach to Azel; yes, you shall flee, just like you fled from before the earthquake in the days of Uzziah king of Judah. Yahweh my God will come, and all the holy ones with you./f + Septuagint reads “him” instead of “you”./f*
echoes.note: 'The LORD my God will come, and all the holy ones with him.' This supplies the retinue of v.31, 'the Son of Man comes in his glory, and all the holy angels with him,' for the day of the LORD's appearing.

echoes.text: “If I have withheld the poor from their desire, or have caused the eyes of the widow to fail, or have eaten my morsel alone, and the fatherless has not eaten of it (no, from my youth he grew up with me as with a father, her have I guided from my mother’s womb); if I have seen any perish for want of clothing, or that the needy had no covering; if his heart hasn’t blessed me, if he hasn’t been warmed with my sheep’s fleece; if I have lifted up my hand […]
echoes.note: Job's oath of innocence — feeding the hungry, clothing the naked, caring for the needy ('if I have not given the poor their portion... if I have seen any perish for lack of clothing') — supplies a near-checklist of the deeds of mercy that define the sheep.

echoes.text: and if you draw out your soul to the hungry, and satisfy the afflicted soul: then your light shall rise in darkness, and your obscurity be as the noonday;
echoes.note: 'If you pour yourself out for the hungry and satisfy the desire of the afflicted, then shall your light rise in the darkness' reinforces the same Isaian ethic of self-giving to the afflicted as the substance of righteousness rewarded by God.

echoes.text: and has not wronged any, but has restored to the debtor his pledge, has taken nothing by robbery, has given his bread to the hungry, and has covered the naked with a garment;
echoes.note: The righteous man 'gives his bread to the hungry and covers the naked with a garment' — Ezekiel's catalog of the deeds that mark the just from the wicked closely parallels the King's criteria and reinforces the Ezekielian frame already operative in the sheep/goats image.

echoes.text: He who has pity on the poor lends to Yahweh; he will reward him.
echoes.note: 'Whoever is kind to the poor lends to the LORD, and he will repay him for his deed.' This is the precise theology of v.40 — kindness to the least is rendered to the King himself, who repays. The identification of the needy with the divine creditor is the conceptual hinge.

echoes.text: He who oppresses the poor shows contempt for his Maker, but he who is kind to the needy honors him.
echoes.note: 'Whoever oppresses a poor man insults his Maker, but he who is generous to the needy honors him.' The principle that treatment of the poor is treatment of God himself underwrites 'you did it to me' / 'you did not do it to me.'

echoes.text: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.
echoes.note: 'Many who sleep in the dust will awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.' This two-fold eternal destiny is the source for v.46, 'these will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life.'

echoes.text: Also to the poor man stretch out your hand, That your blessing may be perfected. A gift has grace in the sight of every man living; And for a dead man keep not back grace. Be not lacking to those who weep; And mourn with those who mourn. Be not slow to visit a sick man; For by such things you will gain love.
echoes.note: Ben Sira's exhortation to stretch out your hand to the poor, give to the needy, not neglect those who weep, and visit the sick supplies a deuterocanonical catalog of mercy-deeds strikingly close to the King's list (feed, clothe, visit the sick).

echoes.text: For, behold, Yahweh will come with fire, and his chariots shall be like the whirlwind; to render his anger with fierceness, and his rebuke with flames of fire. For by fire will Yahweh execute judgment, and by his sword, on all flesh; and the slain of Yahweh shall be many.
echoes.note: 'The LORD will come with fire... by fire will the LORD enter into judgment with all flesh' faintly underlies the 'eternal fire' prepared for the cursed and the universal judgment of all flesh/nations.

echoes.text: “They shall go out, and look on the dead bodies of the men who have transgressed against me: for their worm shall not die, neither shall their fire be quenched; and they will be loathsome to all mankind.”
echoes.note: The closing image of the unquenched fire / undying worm for the rebellious provides scriptural background for the 'eternal fire' and 'eternal punishment' of v.41, 46.

echoes.text: Yahweh says to my Lord, “Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool for your feet.”
echoes.note: The enthronement of the messianic Lord at God's right hand, with subjugation of enemies, underlies the royal session of the Son of Man on the throne of his glory and the placing of subjects at the right and left.

echoes.text: For he will deliver the needy when he cries; the poor, who has no helper. He will have pity on the poor and needy. He will save the souls of the needy. He will redeem their soul from oppression and violence. Their blood will be precious in his sight.
echoes.note: The royal psalm's portrait of the king who delivers the needy, the poor, and those who have no helper, redeeming their life from oppression, supplies the ideal of the just king whose rule is measured by care for the vulnerable — the standard the King applies.

echoes.text: In this mountain, Yahweh of Armies will make all peoples a feast of fat things, a feast of choice wines, of fat things full of marrow, of well refined choice wines. He will destroy in this mountain the surface of the covering that covers all peoples, and the veil that is spread over all nations. He has swallowed up death forever! The Lord Yahweh will wipe away tears from off all faces. He will take the reproach of his people away from off all the earth, […]
echoes.note: The eschatological banquet on the mountain for all peoples, where death is swallowed up, faintly informs the inheritance/eternal-life reward into which the blessed are welcomed when all nations are gathered.

echoes.text: But the souls of the righteous are in the hand of God, And no torment will touch them. In the eyes of the foolish they seemed to have died; And their departure was accounted to be their hurt, And their journeying away from us to be their ruin: But they are in peace. For even if in the sight of men they be punished, Their hope is full of immortality; And having borne a little chastening, they will receive great good; Because God made trial of them, and […]
echoes.note: The deuterocanonical promise that the righteous are in God's hand, will be vindicated at the visitation, judge nations, and receive a kingdom/crown, parallels the righteous inheriting the kingdom and the eternal-life reward at the eschatological assize.

echoes.text: In the days of Enemessar, I did many alms deeds to my kindred: I gave my bread to the hungry, and my garments to the naked. If I saw any of my race dead, and cast forth on the wall of Ninevah, I buried him.
echoes.note: Tobit's acts of charity — giving bread to the hungry, clothing to the naked, and burying the dead — model the very deeds of mercy that mark the righteous and were understood in Second Temple piety as righteousness stored up before God.

echoes.text: Give alms from your possessions. When you give alms, don’t let your eye be envious. Don’t turn away your face from any poor man, and the face of God won’t be turned away from you. As your possessions are, give alms of it according to your abundance. If you have little, don’t be afraid to give alms according to that little; for you lay up a good treasure for yourself against the day of necessity; because alms-giving delivers from death, and doesn’t allow […]
echoes.note: Tobit's instruction to give alms from your possessions, for almsgiving 'is a good gift in the sight of the Most High' and lays up treasure against the day of necessity, reflects the same logic that deeds to the least are rendered to God and rewarded eschatologically.

echoes.text: Come! Come! Flee from the land of the north,’ says Yahweh; ‘for I have spread you abroad as the four winds of the sky,’ says Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'I have spread you abroad as the four winds' / the scattering and gathering language of Zechariah faintly resonates with the gathering of all nations before the throne, though the dominant gathering source is Joel 3.

echoes.text: In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth.
echoes.note: 'The kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world' (v.34) presupposes the creation account as the temporal anchor — the kingdom planned since the world's founding, a protological framing of the inheritance.

notes.text: In the cloudy and dark day — In the time of general distress.
The fat — The powerful and rich. I will feed - I will judge and punish them.
I will judge — I will vindicate the poor. The fat cattle - The rich. The lean - The poor.

One shepherd — Christ, the great good, chief, only shepherd, that laid down his life for his sheep. My servant David - The seed of David, the beloved one, who was typified by David, and is in other places called by his name, as Jer. xxx, 9 chap. xxxvii, 24 Isaiah xxxvii, 35 Hosea iii, 5. He shall feed - Do all the office of a good and faithful shepherd, and that forever.
My servant — Christ was in this great work his fathers servant, Isaiah xlii, 1.
God's — Above all that are called God's angels, earthly potentates, and especially the false gods of the Heathen.
Hand — Under his government. Strength - The strongest or highest mountains.
Pasture — Whom he feeds and keeps in his own pasture, or in the land which he hath appropriated to himself. The sheep - Which are under his special care. Today - Forthwith or presently.

glossa.text: *Come, let us rejoice.* ((THEOD.)) King Josias was exceedingly pious, etc., *as far as* but the psalm is framed in the person of Josias, and of the priests of God. ((CASS.)) Concerning the time of grace, in which there is an entering into rest, the prophet, describing the praises of God, first invites the Jews, whom he foresaw to be able to resist Christ.

*His face,* etc. ((AUG., CASS.)) The sight of the judge to come, lest there be anything then in us to be sifted. *In confession.* ((AUG.)) Praising him, accusing ourselves, etc., *as far as* of which praise the psalm treats. *In psalms let us make a joyful noise.* *psalmi*; read *psalmis*, "in psalms" What we say in psalms, or do, let us feel in jubilation.
*Above all gods.* Or rather he calls men gods, over whom he is king, not over demons.
*For in his hand,* etc. ((CASS.)) After the greatness of the Lord foretold, he comes to his clemency.

*The sea.* ((AUG.)) The world, whose waves God confines within a bound, not suffering us to be tempted above that which we are able ((I Cor. X)); which waves also make increase for us, God working it, nor do the scandals hurt thee, which receive their measure from God.

*Come, let us adore.* ((CASS.)) First he called the untaught to exultation: now, the glory of God being shown, he calls to penance, which is the harder. *Let us weep.* ((AUG.)) If perchance you are solicitous concerning the sins which have made you far off, weep: a tear extinguishes the flame of sin which burns in the conscience. *Who made us.* Behold great confidence: for of thyself thou canst fail, thyself thou canst not remake, he remakes thee who made thee.

*And we are the people,* etc. ((AUG.)) Elegantly is the order of the words changed: He did not say the sheep of the pasture and the people of his hand, that thou mayest understand those very ones to be sheep who are the people, sheep of his hand, not those which from afar, because they are, and sheep which we did not make, but he himself by his own grace made us sheep.

notes.text: Since I heard of your faith and love — That is, of their perseverance and increase therein.
I cease not — In all my solemn addresses to God. To give thanks for you, making mention of you in my prayers - So he did of all the churches, Col. i, 9.

That the Father of that infinite glory which shines in the face of Christ, from whom also we receive the glorious inheritance, ver. 18, may give you the Spirit of wisdom and Revelation — The same who is the Spirit of promise is also, in the progress of the faithful, the Spirit of wisdom and Revelation; making them wise unto salvation, and revealing to them the deep things of God. He is here speaking of that wisdom and Revelation which are common to all real Christians.

The eyes of your understanding — It is with these alone that we discern the things of God. Being first opened, and then enlightened - By his Spirit. That ye may know what is the hope of his calling - That ye may experimentally and delightfully know what are the blessings which God has called you to hope for by his word and his Spirit. And what is the riches of the glory of his inheritance in the saints - What an immense treasure of blessedness he hath provided as an inheritance for holy souls.

And what the exceeding greatness of his power toward us who believe — Both in quickening our dead souls, and preserving them in spiritual life. According to the power which he exerted in Christ, raising him from the dead - By the very same almighty power whereby he raised Christ; for no less would suffice.

And he hath seated him at his own right hand — That is, he hath exalted him in his human nature, as a recompence for his sufferings, to a quiet, everlasting possession of all possible blessedness, majesty, and glory.

Far above all principality, and power, and might, and dominion — That is, God hath invested him with uncontrollable authority over all demons in hell, all angels in heaven, and all the princes and potentates on earth. And every name that is named - We know the king is above all, though we cannot name all the officers of his court. So we know that Christ is above all, though we are not able to name all his subjects. Not only in this world, but also in that which is to come - The world to come is so styled, not because it does not yet exist, but because it is not yet visible. Principalities and powers are named now; but those also who are not even named in this world, but shall be revealed in the world to come, are all subject to Christ.

And he hath given him to be head over all things to the church — An head both of guidance and government, and likewise of life and influence, to the whole and every member of it. All these stand in the nearest union with him, and have as continual and effectual a communication of activity, growth, and strength from him, as the natural body from its head.

The fulness of him that filleth all in all — It is hard to say in what sense this can be spoken of the church; but the sense is easy and natural, if we refer it to Christ, who is the fulness of the Father.

glossa.text: *Therefore.* The benefits conferred upon the human race, or upon the apostles, or upon the Ephesians having been enumerated, the Apostle subjoins what he thinks concerning their benefits, namely that he gives thanks, and asks that more be added, lest they be proud, but stretch beyond.
*That God,* etc. As if he should say: to obtain it I put forward not merits, but that he is God and the Father of Christ, etc.

*The eyes of the heart.* In his own image, therefore, know thou its author, who is not attained by bodily sense. Do not, therefore, think that God is attained by bodily sense, but with the eyes of the mind hear him. In the body, where the members are diverse, thou hearest in one place, thou seest in another. But in thy heart, where diverse members are not found, there thou hearest where thou seest. And to this end may he enlighten the eyes. *That you may know,* etc. This he says that they may be the more inclined: because when they shall fully know what the fruit of believers is, they will become the more inclined toward the cultivating of religion. Or thus: that hope be taken properly. And the sense is: That you may know what it is, namely his will *voluntas*; read *vocatio*, "calling", that is, how much the hope of eternal life avails, unto which he calls. And that you may know what the fulfilment of that hope is. Which he thus says: *And what are the riches.* Here he discloses what he understood by the name of hope: for he takes hope as the thing hoped for.

*What is the exceeding greatness.* The highest doctors shall have a certain increase of glory, beyond that which all shall have in common. For all shall have the same penny. *But star differeth from star in brightness ((I Cor. XV))*. *And there shall be diverse mansions in the house of the Father ((Joan. XIV))*.

*Raising him up,* etc. Now the example of the glory of the saints consists in the resurrection of the Saviour, that in it the faithful may know what has been promised to them. *At his right hand.* The right hand is the eternal beatitude which is given to the saints: the left is the misery which is given to the wicked. For by no form of body is God bounded and enclosed.

*Above every,* etc. This he says on account of the incarnation of the Son of God, that even having been made man he may be said to be above all the heavens, and above every creature, having his name by nature, not by adoption.

*Under his feet,* etc. By the feet full subjection is noted, and all things are deservedly subject to him, because they were made through him; or, the feet signify the humanity, because as the foot is the lower part of the body, so in Christ the lower nature is the humanity, which even the angels adore. *And him,* etc. After he has commemorated the dignity of Christ, he returns to us, showing that his dignity pertains to us; as if he should say: God so exalted Christ that this his exaltation pertains to us: because he himself is the head, and we the body, that we may partake of him. *The head.* According to the deity: because all were made by him, and also according to the humanity, by which the Church is joined to him, by nature and by grace. *For of his fullness we have all received ((Joan. X))*.

*His fullness.* Because he is filled up through them, yet being all things in all, here and in the time to come. Likewise. When those who have entered unto confession bend the knee to Christ, he is filled up, because those who withdraw seem to empty him. *All things in all.* Because the members confer nothing upon him, but he himself all things upon the members: because by his power they are what they are.

notes.text: Inherit the kingdom — Purchased by my blood, for all who have believed in me with the faith which wrought by love. Prepared for you - On purpose for you. May it not be probably inferred from hence, that man was not created merely to fill up the places of the fallen angels?

I was hungry, and ye gave me meat; I was thirsty, and ye gave me drink — All these works of outward mercy suppose faith and love, and must needs he accompanied with works of spiritual mercy. But works of this kind the Judge could not mention in the same manner. He could not say, I was in error, and ye recalled me to the truth; I was in sin, and ye brought me to repentance. In prison - Prisoners need to be visited above all others, as they are commonly solitary and forsaken by the rest of the world.

Then shall the righteous answer — It cannot be, that either the righteous or the wicked should answer in these very words. What we learn herefrom is, that neither of them have the same estimation of their own works as the Judge hath.
Inasmuch as ye did it to one of the least of these my brethren, ye did it to me — What encouragement is here to assist the household of faith? But let us likewise remember to do good to all men.
Depart into the everlasting fire, which was prepared for the devil and his angels — Not originally for you: you are intruders into everlasting fire.
Then will they answer — So the endeavour to justify themselves, will remain with the wicked even to that day!

And these shall go away into everlasting punishment, but the righteous into life everlasting — Either therefore the punishment is strictly eternal, or the reward is not: the very same expression being applied to the former as to the latter. The Judge will speak first to the righteous, in the audience of the wicked. The wicked shall then go away into everlasting fire, in the view of the righteous. Thus the damned shall see nothing of the everlasting life; but the just will see the punishment of the ungodly. It is not only particularly observable here

1. That the punishment lasts as long as the reward; but,

2. That this punishment is so far from ceasing at the end of the world, that it does not begin till then.

glossa.text: *And when.* Being about to be delivered to the cross very soon, he set before them the glory of him who triumphs, that he might make up by this promise for the scandals that were to follow. After the parables about the end of the world, the Lord now sets forth the manner of the judgment to come.

*The sheep from,* etc. There shall be two orders in the judgment, namely of the elect and of the reprobate: but of the elect some shall judge, to whom it is said: *You also shall sit upon twelve seats, judging the tribes of Israel.* Others shall be judged, to whom it is said: *I was hungry and you gave me to eat.* Likewise of the reprobate, some who are outside the Church shall not be judged: others who shall be judged, to whom it is said: *I was hungry, and you gave me not to eat,* etc.
*The goats.* The he-goat is a butting and rank-smelling animal, which was offered for sins in the law, and it signifies sinners: nor does he say she-goats, which can have young.

*Blessed of the Father.* Advanced by the benefit of my Father to the obtaining of glory, in which you may reign without corruption, to which you have been predestined from the foundation of the world.

*Then shall they answer.* Not distrusting the words of the Lord, but either amazed at the greatness of the king's majesty; or because every good thing that they did seems little to them, whence it is said: *The sufferings of this time are not worthy to be compared with the glory to come ((Rom. VIII))*, etc.
*Of these brethren.* My brethren and my mother are they who do the will of my Father.
*You gave me not,* etc. What does he deserve who has seized what belongs to another, if he is eternally damned who has not given anything of his own?

*Lord, when,* etc. They busy themselves to excuse themselves, as though they who were deceiving men could deceive God. But they have no excuse who would not be converted from evils and do alms; whence he adds: *As long as you did it not to one,* etc.

*Into everlasting punishment.* In vain therefore does Origen promise deliverance after many years to evil men and to the demons themselves. *Into everlasting punishment. ((AUG.))* In which matter Origen was assuredly the more merciful, who believed that the devil himself too and his angels, after punishments heavier according to their deserts and of longer duration, were to be rescued out of those torments and joined to the holy angels. But the Church has not undeservedly condemned him, both for this and for sundry other things, and chiefly for the blessednesses and miseries alternating without ceasing, and for the endless goings and returnings from those to these at fixed intervals of ages.

echoes.text: The Spirit of Yahweh will rest on him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and of the fear of Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'A spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him' draws on the Messianic 'Spirit of the LORD... the spirit of wisdom and understanding... the spirit of knowledge.' Volume is strong (spirit + wisdom + knowledge in sequence); thematic coherence (the endowing Spirit granting wisdom and knowledge of God) and the passage's Messianic availability make this a high-confidence allusion.

echoes.text: He changes the times and the seasons; he removes kings, and sets up kings; he gives wisdom to the wise, and knowledge to those who have understanding; he reveals the deep and secret things; he knows what is in the darkness, and the light dwells with him.
echoes.note: 'A spirit of wisdom and revelation' coheres with Daniel's God who 'gives wisdom to the wise... reveals deep and hidden things.' Recurrence of the Danielic wisdom/revelation pairing (cf. 1:9 mystery) supports a medium echo; the volume is moderate alongside the dominant Isaiah 11 source.

echoes.text: For this cause I prayed, and understanding was given me: I called upon God, and there came to me a spirit of wisdom.
echoes.note: 'I prayed, and understanding was given me; I called, and the spirit of wisdom came to me' (deuterocanonical) closely parallels praying for 'a spirit of wisdom' to know God. Thematic coherence is strong and the Wisdom tradition was available in Greek-speaking Judaism; medium because it is a parallel within a shared milieu rather than a citation.

echoes.text: You shall speak to all who are wise-hearted, whom I have filled with the spirit of wisdom, that they make Aaron’s garments to sanctify him, that he may minister to me in the priest’s office.
echoes.note: God filling artisans with a 'spirit of wisdom' to equip them is one OT background for Spirit-given wisdom granted to God's people. Availability is real but thematic coherence with revelatory knowledge of God is weaker than Isaiah 11; marked low and contested.

echoes.text: He filled them with the knowledge of wisdom, And showed them good and evil. He set his eye upon their hearts, To show them the majesty of his works.
echoes.note: Sirach's depiction of God enlightening humans with knowledge and 'setting his eye on their hearts' resonates faintly with 'the eyes of your hearts enlightened.' Availability within the wisdom corpus is genuine; volume and verbal overlap are low, so the echo is contested.

echoes.text: Yahweh’s precepts are right, rejoicing the heart. Yahweh’s commandment is pure, enlightening the eyes.
echoes.note: 'The commandment of the LORD is pure, enlightening the eyes' offers an OT idiom of divine illumination behind 'the eyes of your hearts enlightened.' Thematic coherence (God enlightening the perceiving faculty) is plausible; volume is faint, so low and contested.

echoes.text: Yahweh says to my Lord, “Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool for your feet.”
echoes.note: 'Made him to sit at his right hand in the heavenly places, far above all rule and authority' reproduces 'Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies your footstool.' Volume is very high (the most-cited OT verse in the NT); recurrence and thematic coherence (enthroned exaltation over all powers) make this a near-quotation undergirding the entire exaltation statement.

echoes.text: You make him ruler over the works of your hands. You have put all things under his feet:
echoes.note: 'He put all things in subjection under his feet' is a verbatim citation of 'you have put all things under his feet.' Volume is maximal (direct verbal match); recurrence (1 Cor 15:27; Heb 2:8) and thematic coherence (the dominion granted to the exalted man over creation) make this an explicit quotation.

echoes.text: Yahweh says to my Lord, “Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool for your feet.”
echoes.note: 'He put all things in subjection under his feet' also fulfills Psalm 110:1's 'until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet,' which Ephesians conflates with Psalm 8:6. The footstool/subjection imagery shows the two enthronement psalms read together; volume and thematic coherence (subjugation of enemies under the exalted Lord) are high.

echoes.text: so that the priests could not stand to minister by reason of the cloud; for Yahweh’s glory filled Yahweh’s house.
echoes.note: 'The fullness of him who fills all in all' evokes the glory of the LORD filling the temple so that 'the priests could not stand to minister.' Thematic coherence (divine presence filling God's house, now the church as body/temple) is strong; medium because the link is conceptual and joins other temple-glory texts.

echoes.text: Can any hide himself in secret places so that I shall not see him? says Yahweh. Don’t I fill heaven and earth? says Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'Do I not fill heaven and earth? says the LORD' supplies the divine self-description behind 'him who fills all in all.' Thematic coherence with God's omnipresent fullness is strong; the volume is moderate (a shared plerosis motif), so medium confidence.

echoes.text: In the year that king Uzziah died, I saw the Lord sitting on a throne, high and lifted up; and his train filled the temple. Above him stood the seraphim. Each one had six wings. With two he covered his face. With two he covered his feet. With two he flew. One called to another, and said, “Holy, holy, holy, is Yahweh of Armies! The whole earth is full of his glory!”
echoes.note: 'The whole earth is full of his glory,' with the temple filled by the LORD's train, reinforces the fullness/glory imagery of 1:23. Availability and thematic coherence (glory filling the sanctuary) support a faint echo; volume is low alongside 1 Kings 8 and Jeremiah 23, so contested.

echoes.text: Yahweh, our Lord, how majestic is your name in all the earth, who has set your glory above the heavens!
echoes.note: 'Head over all things' resonates with Psalm 8's exaltation of God's name 'above the heavens' and the dominion theme framing the quoted v.6. Thematic coherence (universal supremacy) is plausible; the volume is low and the link secondary to 8:6, so contested.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.
echoes.note: The Son of Man coming in glory and seated on his throne, before whom all nations/peoples are gathered to serve him, is the direct backbone of v.31-32. Daniel's 'one like a son of man' receives dominion, glory, and kingdom over all peoples, nations, and languages; Matthew transposes this enthronement into the scene of universal judgment.

echoes.text: As for you, O my flock, thus says the Lord Yahweh: Behold, I judge between sheep and sheep, the rams and the male goats.
echoes.note: 'I judge between sheep and sheep, between rams and goats' is the explicit verbal and conceptual source for 'he will separate them... as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats' (v.32-33). The shepherd-judge distinguishing the flock animals is unmistakable.

echoes.text: Therefore thus says the Lord Yahweh to them: Behold, I, even I, will judge between the fat sheep and the lean sheep. Because you thrust with side and with shoulder, and push all the diseased with your horns, until you have scattered them abroad; therefore will I save my flock, and they shall no more be a prey; and I will judge between sheep and sheep.
echoes.note: The LORD 'will judge between the fat sheep and the lean sheep,' saving the weak from those who shove with side and shoulder. This grounds the criterion of judgment on treatment of the vulnerable and the shepherd-king's vindication of the mistreated, mirrored in care for the hungry, naked, sick, and imprisoned.

echoes.text: I will set up one shepherd over them, and he shall feed them, even my servant David; he shall feed them, and he shall be their shepherd. I, Yahweh, will be their God, and my servant David prince among them; I, Yahweh, have spoken it.
echoes.note: The promise of one shepherd, 'my servant David,' set over the flock as prince, is typologically fulfilled in the Son of Man / King who shepherds and judges the nations. The Davidic shepherd-king of Ezekiel 34 is the figure Matthew casts Jesus as embodying.

echoes.text: Isn’t it to distribute your bread to the hungry, and that you bring the poor who are cast out to your house? When you see the naked, that you cover him; and that you not hide yourself from your own flesh?
echoes.note: The acts of true fasting/righteousness — 'share your bread with the hungry, bring the homeless poor into your house, when you see the naked, cover him' — closely match the King's catalog of hungry/stranger/naked in v.35-36. Isaiah 58 is the strongest verbal parallel for the works that mark the righteous.

echoes.text: I will gather all nations, and will bring them down into the valley of Jehoshaphat; and I will execute judgment on them there for my people, and for my heritage, Israel, whom they have scattered among the nations. They have divided my land,
echoes.note: 'I will gather all the nations... and I will enter into judgment with them there' supplies the assize of the nations gathered before the throne (v.32), where they are judged on how they treated God's people.

echoes.text: “Let the nations arouse themselves, and come up to the valley of Jehoshaphat; for there will I sit to judge all the surrounding nations.
echoes.note: 'Let the nations be roused and come up to the valley of Jehoshaphat, for there I will sit to judge all the surrounding nations.' The enthroned divine Judge seated to judge the assembled nations directly parallels the Son of Man sitting on the throne of his glory to judge all the nations.

echoes.text: You shall flee by the valley of my mountains; for the valley of the mountains shall reach to Azel; yes, you shall flee, just like you fled from before the earthquake in the days of Uzziah king of Judah. Yahweh my God will come, and all the holy ones with you./f + Septuagint reads “him” instead of “you”./f*
echoes.note: 'The LORD my God will come, and all the holy ones with him.' This supplies the retinue of v.31, 'the Son of Man comes in his glory, and all the holy angels with him,' for the day of the LORD's appearing.

echoes.text: “If I have withheld the poor from their desire, or have caused the eyes of the widow to fail, or have eaten my morsel alone, and the fatherless has not eaten of it (no, from my youth he grew up with me as with a father, her have I guided from my mother’s womb); if I have seen any perish for want of clothing, or that the needy had no covering; if his heart hasn’t blessed me, if he hasn’t been warmed with my sheep’s fleece; if I have lifted up my hand […]
echoes.note: Job's oath of innocence — feeding the hungry, clothing the naked, caring for the needy ('if I have not given the poor their portion... if I have seen any perish for lack of clothing') — supplies a near-checklist of the deeds of mercy that define the sheep.

echoes.text: and if you draw out your soul to the hungry, and satisfy the afflicted soul: then your light shall rise in darkness, and your obscurity be as the noonday;
echoes.note: 'If you pour yourself out for the hungry and satisfy the desire of the afflicted, then shall your light rise in the darkness' reinforces the same Isaian ethic of self-giving to the afflicted as the substance of righteousness rewarded by God.

echoes.text: and has not wronged any, but has restored to the debtor his pledge, has taken nothing by robbery, has given his bread to the hungry, and has covered the naked with a garment;
echoes.note: The righteous man 'gives his bread to the hungry and covers the naked with a garment' — Ezekiel's catalog of the deeds that mark the just from the wicked closely parallels the King's criteria and reinforces the Ezekielian frame already operative in the sheep/goats image.

echoes.text: He who has pity on the poor lends to Yahweh; he will reward him.
echoes.note: 'Whoever is kind to the poor lends to the LORD, and he will repay him for his deed.' This is the precise theology of v.40 — kindness to the least is rendered to the King himself, who repays. The identification of the needy with the divine creditor is the conceptual hinge.

echoes.text: He who oppresses the poor shows contempt for his Maker, but he who is kind to the needy honors him.
echoes.note: 'Whoever oppresses a poor man insults his Maker, but he who is generous to the needy honors him.' The principle that treatment of the poor is treatment of God himself underwrites 'you did it to me' / 'you did not do it to me.'

echoes.text: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.
echoes.note: 'Many who sleep in the dust will awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.' This two-fold eternal destiny is the source for v.46, 'these will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life.'

echoes.text: Also to the poor man stretch out your hand, That your blessing may be perfected. A gift has grace in the sight of every man living; And for a dead man keep not back grace. Be not lacking to those who weep; And mourn with those who mourn. Be not slow to visit a sick man; For by such things you will gain love.
echoes.note: Ben Sira's exhortation to stretch out your hand to the poor, give to the needy, not neglect those who weep, and visit the sick supplies a deuterocanonical catalog of mercy-deeds strikingly close to the King's list (feed, clothe, visit the sick).

echoes.text: For, behold, Yahweh will come with fire, and his chariots shall be like the whirlwind; to render his anger with fierceness, and his rebuke with flames of fire. For by fire will Yahweh execute judgment, and by his sword, on all flesh; and the slain of Yahweh shall be many.
echoes.note: 'The LORD will come with fire... by fire will the LORD enter into judgment with all flesh' faintly underlies the 'eternal fire' prepared for the cursed and the universal judgment of all flesh/nations.

echoes.text: “They shall go out, and look on the dead bodies of the men who have transgressed against me: for their worm shall not die, neither shall their fire be quenched; and they will be loathsome to all mankind.”
echoes.note: The closing image of the unquenched fire / undying worm for the rebellious provides scriptural background for the 'eternal fire' and 'eternal punishment' of v.41, 46.

echoes.text: Yahweh says to my Lord, “Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool for your feet.”
echoes.note: The enthronement of the messianic Lord at God's right hand, with subjugation of enemies, underlies the royal session of the Son of Man on the throne of his glory and the placing of subjects at the right and left.

echoes.text: For he will deliver the needy when he cries; the poor, who has no helper. He will have pity on the poor and needy. He will save the souls of the needy. He will redeem their soul from oppression and violence. Their blood will be precious in his sight.
echoes.note: The royal psalm's portrait of the king who delivers the needy, the poor, and those who have no helper, redeeming their life from oppression, supplies the ideal of the just king whose rule is measured by care for the vulnerable — the standard the King applies.

echoes.text: In this mountain, Yahweh of Armies will make all peoples a feast of fat things, a feast of choice wines, of fat things full of marrow, of well refined choice wines. He will destroy in this mountain the surface of the covering that covers all peoples, and the veil that is spread over all nations. He has swallowed up death forever! The Lord Yahweh will wipe away tears from off all faces. He will take the reproach of his people away from off all the earth, […]
echoes.note: The eschatological banquet on the mountain for all peoples, where death is swallowed up, faintly informs the inheritance/eternal-life reward into which the blessed are welcomed when all nations are gathered.

echoes.text: But the souls of the righteous are in the hand of God, And no torment will touch them. In the eyes of the foolish they seemed to have died; And their departure was accounted to be their hurt, And their journeying away from us to be their ruin: But they are in peace. For even if in the sight of men they be punished, Their hope is full of immortality; And having borne a little chastening, they will receive great good; Because God made trial of them, and […]
echoes.note: The deuterocanonical promise that the righteous are in God's hand, will be vindicated at the visitation, judge nations, and receive a kingdom/crown, parallels the righteous inheriting the kingdom and the eternal-life reward at the eschatological assize.

echoes.text: In the days of Enemessar, I did many alms deeds to my kindred: I gave my bread to the hungry, and my garments to the naked. If I saw any of my race dead, and cast forth on the wall of Ninevah, I buried him.
echoes.note: Tobit's acts of charity — giving bread to the hungry, clothing to the naked, and burying the dead — model the very deeds of mercy that mark the righteous and were understood in Second Temple piety as righteousness stored up before God.

echoes.text: Give alms from your possessions. When you give alms, don’t let your eye be envious. Don’t turn away your face from any poor man, and the face of God won’t be turned away from you. As your possessions are, give alms of it according to your abundance. If you have little, don’t be afraid to give alms according to that little; for you lay up a good treasure for yourself against the day of necessity; because alms-giving delivers from death, and doesn’t allow […]
echoes.note: Tobit's instruction to give alms from your possessions, for almsgiving 'is a good gift in the sight of the Most High' and lays up treasure against the day of necessity, reflects the same logic that deeds to the least are rendered to God and rewarded eschatologically.

echoes.text: Come! Come! Flee from the land of the north,’ says Yahweh; ‘for I have spread you abroad as the four winds of the sky,’ says Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'I have spread you abroad as the four winds' / the scattering and gathering language of Zechariah faintly resonates with the gathering of all nations before the throne, though the dominant gathering source is Joel 3.

echoes.text: In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth.
echoes.note: 'The kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world' (v.34) presupposes the creation account as the temporal anchor — the kingdom planned since the world's founding, a protological framing of the inheritance.

registers.label: Spare
lines: Come, let us sing to the Lord, the great King above all gods.
We are his people, the sheep of his hand.
The Son of Man will come in glory and sit on his throne.
And he will know us by our mercy to the least.
God has seated Christ far above every rule and power.
He is head over all things for the church.
Come, let us worship Christ the King.
We bow before the Shepherd-King. Amen.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: Lift your eyes to the throne at the end of all things, the Son of Man crowned in glory, the nations gathered before him like a shepherd dividing the flock.
Christ is King, and we are his.
Yet this King is the Shepherd who searches for the lost, binds up the broken, and carries the weak ones home.
Christ is King, and we are his.
He has been raised far above every ruler and power and given a name above every name, head over all things for us.
Christ is King, and we are his.
And he is known by this: a cup of water, a coat, a visit to the prison — as you did it to the least, you did it to the King.
Christ is King, and we are his.
So come, you sheep of his pasture, and bow before the Shepherd-King.
Christ is King, and we are his! Alleluia!

registers.label: Hybrid
lines: Come, sing to the Lord, the great King above all.
Christ is King, and we are his.
The Son of Man comes in glory to the throne.
Christ is King, and we are his.
This King is the Shepherd who seeks the lost.
Christ is King, and we are his.
Come, let us worship Christ the King.
We bow before the Shepherd-King. Amen.
